title: Dozens of Israelis stranded in Nepali village after landslide and flooding - The Jewish Chronicle
description: Dozens of Israelis stranded in Nepali village after landslide and flooding  The Jewish Chronicle
publisher.title: The Jewish Chronicle
full_article:
Nepal has been hit by further flooding and landslides only weeks after a flash flood in which more than 1,400 people were killed and thousands, including two Israelis, were reported missing.

Some of the Israelis sheltering in Samagaun described hearing landslides and rockfalls close to the village.

“Every few hours we hear a huge boom, as if the ground is totally collapsing,” one Israeli tourist told public broadcaster Kan.

Another told Ynet : “Our lives were saved by a miracle. We have no way to go back or move forward because bridges have collapsed and roads are blocked. There is a real danger to our lives, since any additional landslide could cause flooding and destroy the village.”

A third traveller said: “We hope to be evacuated from here before dark. I’m afraid a terrible disaster will happen. There are landslides here every few hours, right over our heads. There’s no need to wait for a disaster to happen.”

Israeli siblings Maya Lamdan, 27, and Nadav Lamdan, 21, were evacuated by helicopter from Samagaun on Sunday and flown to Kathmandu, according to The Jerusalem Post .

Travel insurance company PassportCard said it was assisting dozens of Israeli tourists in Nepal and that none were believed to be in life-threatening condition at the time of its assessment.

The Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the Israeli embassy in Nepal “is in contact with tour companies and local guides, and is working to locate Israelis who have not yet been reached, as well as to provide assistance, insofar as possible and subject to conditions on the ground, in efforts to move them to safe areas”.

The ministry also warned Israelis against trekking and mountaineering in the country while the dangerous conditions persisted, saying recent weather had caused road closures and widespread disruption to transport.

The UK government has similarly warned that areas affected by the August flooding and landslides may remain unstable, with further heavy rain capable of triggering additional landslides and rockfalls, particularly in mountainous regions.

Nepali authorities have again warned of the threat of flash flooding, with 49 of the country's 77 districts identified as potentially at risk as river levels rose.

The latest storms have also caused deaths elsewhere in the region. In northern India, at least 62 people had died in Uttar Pradesh following days of heavy rain and flooding, according to Associated Press reporting.

In Nepal's Manang district, meanwhile, an avalanche struck the base camp of Himlung Himal, a 7,126-metre peak, where Nepali workers and guides had been preparing for the climbing season.

The death toll from that avalanche rose to four on Monday, while 12 people remained missing, according to the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association.

Search teams were operating from the base camp by helicopter, although heavy snow and rain were making the operation hazardous.

The Israeli embassy in Kathmandu has continued to provide consular assistance and maintain contact with local authorities, tour companies and guides.

title: Avalanche at Himlung Himal in Nepal leaves 2 dead, 14 missing - DW.com
description: Avalanche at Himlung Himal in Nepal leaves 2 dead, 14 missing  DW.com
publisher.title: DW.com
full_article:
Two people have died when an avalanche struck the base camp of a mountain in Nepal with at least 14 others still missing.

The avalanche hit the 7,126-meter (23,380-foot) Himlung Himal after several days of heavy rain and snowfall across the region.

The dead and missing are all mountain guides and staff of Nepalese expedition companies who had been preparing the base camp for paying customers to climb the mountain.

"There were a total of 14 kitchen staff members and two climbing guides from different companies who were missing," the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association said. "The two climbing guides have been found, but sadly, both were found deceased."

Unclear how many are missing

There was conflicting information as to how many people were in the affected area near the border with Tibet at the time of disaster. Local police said there were at least 22 people at the base camp when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.

Bibhuti Chand Thakur, head of trekking company Himalayan Holidays Nepal, told news agency DPA that search and rescue operations were under way. "The chance of survival remains high because of fresh snow," he said, adding that he did not yet have a definitive number of missing or survivors, as the area is remote and cut off from communication.

While Mount Everest (pictured) is Nepal's most famous peak, peaks like Himlung Himal are also popular with climbers [FILE: May 21, 2024] Image: Narendra Shahi Thakuri/dpa/picture alliance

Authorities had warned of severe weather across Nepal over the weekend. Rain has affected much of the country since Thursday, with snowfall reported in the higher northern regions. The conditions have disrupted roads and trekking routes and led authorities to suspend climbing and trekking activities on several mountains.

The Himalayan nation is home to eight of the world's 14 mountains higher than 8,000 meters, and trekking and mountaineering tourism is vital to the country's economy.

The latest avalanche comes as Nepal continues to recover from devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

title: Nepal promotes tourism recovery at Tourism Expo Japan 2026 - The Tourism Times
description: Nepal promotes tourism recovery at Tourism Expo Japan 2026  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal Tourism Board (NTB), together with nine travel and hospitality companies and Nepal Airlines Corporation, participated in Tourism Expo Japan 2026 in Tokyo from Sept. 24 to 27, using the platform to promote Nepal's tourism recovery and strengthen ties with the Japanese travel market.

The international travel expo, organised by the Japan Travel and Tourism Association, Japan Association of Travel Agents and Japan National Tourism Organization, brought together around 1,420 tourism companies and organisations from 74 countries under the theme “The Changing Nature of Travel.”

During the four-day event, NTB officials provided international travel buyers, tour operators and media representatives with updates on Nepal's tourism sector following recent monsoon-related disasters in parts of the country.

According to the board, the Nepali delegation informed participants that major tourism hubs including Kathmandu, Pokhara, Chitwan and Lumbini remain fully operational, while key trekking destinations such as the Everest, Annapurna, Langtang and Manaslu regions continue to welcome visitors.

The expo also served as a venue for business-to-business (B2B) meetings between Nepali tourism entrepreneurs and Japanese travel companies. Discussions focused on trekking, cultural tourism, spiritual travel, wellness experiences and other tourism products.

NTB Senior Officers Pradip Gaire and Yub Raj Gurung represented the board at the event. Nepal's pavilion also featured participation from Nepal Airlines Corporation and nine private-sector tourism companies.

The participating companies included:

Gochali Tours and Travels

Sumegh Tours and Travels

Himalayan Guides Nepal Treks & Expedition

Langtang Ri Trekking & Expedition

Ghale Treks & Expedition

Buddha Maya Gardens

Rupakot Resort

Chhaya Devi Complex (Aloft Kathmandu Thamel)

Gorkha International Travels

The Embassy of Nepal in Tokyo supported Nepal's participation in the event.

According to the NTB, the expo was also used to promote the board's Nepalcalling campaign and Nepal Wellness Year 2026, aimed at attracting more international visitors and strengthening Nepal's image as a destination for adventure, culture, spirituality and wellness tourism.

The participation comes as Nepal seeks to reassure global tourism markets that its major destinations remain accessible and prepared to receive international visitors despite localized impacts from recent monsoon-related disasters.

title: A Remarkable Child Who Connected Nepal to the Buddhist World - Tibetan Review
description: A Remarkable Child Who Connected Nepal to the Buddhist World  Tibetan Review
publisher.title: Tibetan Review
full_article:
Nepal honoured Bhrikuti, Bhelsa Tritsun in Tibetan, who was married to Tibet’s 33rd Yarlung Dynasty King Songtsen Gampo, the founder of the 7th to 9th century Tibetan empire, as a N ational Luminary in 1955 for being a bearer of Nepal’s Buddhist culture and a symbol of peace, but then removed her from the list in 2017, ostensibly due to lack of sufficient historical records about her in the country’s archives. Now, as a case is sought to be made to restore her status with a twist to colour her contributions in light of Kathmandu’s current One China policy stand, Biswo Ulak* gives an account of her as a real historical figure who carried the teachings of the Buddha from Nepal to Tibet and beyond, with a hope to encourage younger generations to appreciate the deep civilisational ties between Nepal and Tibet.

At just eight years of age, Bhrikuti left her homeland on a remarkable journey to Tibet, carrying the Nepali Buddhist culture and traditions. Through her marriage to King Songtsen Gampo and the cultural exchange that followed, the influence of Nepali Buddhism reached in Tibet and eventually extended into China and other parts of East and Southeast Asia. Her history was largely overlooked in Nepal because, according to this account, she was born in Kurpasi (Khopasi) while her family was living in exile, outside the Kathmandu Valley.

French Professor Sylvain Lévi, who was among the first scholars to write about Nepal’s history, has made a mention of Bribtsn, the daughter of the Nepali king Go Cha (a Tibetan term meaning “Rising Light”) from the Tibetan and Chinese chronology. However, he suspected that her father might have been Amshuvarma Thakuri, as he was the most powerful and influential ruler of Nepal during that period, although Lévi did not reach a definitive conclusion. Nepali historian Baburam Acharya renamed Bribtsn as Bhrikuti Devi and described her as the daughter of Amshuvarma Thakuri, an interpretation later followed by several other contemporary scholars. However, Lilabhakta Munankarmi was not convinced that Bhrikuti was Amshuvarma Thakuri’s daughter. In an article published in Gorkhapatra in 2020 BS, historian Bhuvan Pradhan presented Bhrikuti as the daughter of Lichhivi King Udaya Deva. ((Editor’s note: BS stands for Bikram Sambat [also spelled Vikram Samvat[, which is the official historical calendar used in Nepal.)

Unfortunately, some Nepali scholars have questioned whether there was a princess named Bhrikuti in Nepal, suggesting that she was merely a fictional character. The Government of Nepal’s Ministry of Education, through the Janak Education Materials Centre, introduced Bhrikuti as the daughter of Amshuvarma Thakuri in the Grade 7 textbook Mahendramala, published in 2031 BS. This conflicting claim appears to have been incorporated into the school curriculum without adequate historical verification. As a result, despite Bhrikuti having been honoured with the title of “National Luminary” in 2012 BS, her historical legacy was later diminished when her name was removed from the list of National Luminaries without a detailed study by the authorities responsible for making such decisions.

The Bhrikuti Smriti Pratisthan subsequently conducted a number of studies on Bhrikuti’s life and historical background in Nepal, including a year-long rigorous details study with the financial support from the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation. The study established her birthplace and identified her parents, findings that were subsequently recognized and accepted by the Government of Nepal. The following are the key findings of the study:

According to traditions, Amshuvarma Thakuri was born in Kurpasi in the 550s AD and became a Samanta (feudal lord of a principality) following the death of his father, Manvarma, in the 570s AD. He continued to serve as a Samanta when the Licchhavi King Shiva Deva I ascended to the throne of Nepal in 590 AD. Local legends say that Amshuvarma Thakuri resided in the former residence of King Birat in Kurpasi, on the present-day premises of Narasingh Math, while his administrative office was located in the then palace of Kailash on the banks of Jhilpu Khola.

King Shiva Deva faced growing challenges to his governance as the influence of the Guptas increased. To counter this influence, he established a matrimonial alliance with the powerful Samanta Amshuvarma Thakuri by giving his daughter to him in marriage around 595 AD. He also sent his eldest son, Prince Udaya Deva, and his wife, Bhadrawati Devi, to Kurpasi to stay with Amshuvarma Thakuri, receiving knowledge and skills of governance. Considering Amshuvarma Thakuri’s competence, integrity, and matrimonial connection with the royal family, King Shiva Deva granted him greater authority in 598 AD through a royal inscription, elevating him to the position of Maha-Samanta (Great Samanta) and later allowing him to exercise de facto kingly authority. He effectively entrusted Amshuvarma Thakuri with the affairs of the kingdom, as King Shiva Deva devoted much of his time to religious and spiritual activities.

Following the death of King Shiva Deva, Amshuvarma Thakuri, who had already been exercising de facto authority, declared himself Maharajadhiraja (King) in 605 AD, reportedly because Prince Udaya Deva was considered unable to govern effectively. However, as Amshuvarma Thakuri had no children of his own, Udaya Deva was reinstated as Crown Prince in 613 AD. Prince Udaya Deva ascended to the throne in 621 AD following the death of Amshuvarma Thakuri, who died at the age of 70 after a long life. Unfortunately, Udaya Deva was unable to withstand the growing influence and attacks from his own brother, Dhrubadeva, who was supported by Jishnu Gupta, Bishnu Gupta, and others. As a result, Udaya Deva was overthrown and removed from the throne in 623 AD.

King Udaya Deva, Queen Bhadrawati Devi, and their one-year-old son, Prince Narendradeva, went into exile and sought refuge at Bhadrawati’s maternal home in Manjushree Tole, Lagan, Kathmandu. According to the tradition presented in the study, Bhrikuti was conceived there in Queen Bhadrawati’s womb while they were in Bhadrawati’s maternal home.

Exiled King Udaya Deva attempted to regain the throne through a revolt, but he was unsuccessful. He was subsequently driven out of Kathmandu and moved to Patan, where he made another attempt to regain his power, but again failed. He then moved to Bhaktapur. After this attempt also proved unsuccessful, the exile royal family moved to Kurpasi, where they settled in the former residence of the Mahasamanta, Amshuvarma Thakuri. This was the place where Udaya Deva and his wife had previously stayed while gaining knowledge and skills of governance. According to traditions, Bhrikuti was born in Kurpasi in 624 AD in the former residence of Amshuvarma Thakuri.

Bhrikuti was raised and groomed in a Buddhist cultural environment, deeply influenced by the traditions of the Kirat and Thakuri periods and the local Pahari inhabitants. In 632 AD, at the age of eight, Bhrikuti was sent to Tibet to marry King Songtsen Gampo, accompanied by a Tibetan delegation led by the Tibetan ministers Thonmi Sambhota and Gar Tongtsen. The ancient route through the Rasuwa Pass was used to take her to Lhasa, and the journey included a pilgrimage to Gosaikunda, which was regarded as an important pilgrimage center for Tibetans. The journey to Lhasa took more than six months. Upon her arrival in Lhasa, Bhrikuti formally married King Songtsen Gampo in 633 AD, at the age of nine.

After Bhrikuti’s departure, the royal palace in Kathmandu continued to persecute the exiled King Udaya Deva. As a result, he could no longer remain in Kurpasi and left for Lhasa with his wife, Queen Bhadrawati Devi, and their son, Prince Narendra Deva, seeking political asylum. They reached Lhasa after Bhrikuti’s formal marriage with King Songtsen Gampo.

An opportunity subsequently arose for Prince Narendra Deva to seek Chinese support for the release of a Chinese envoy from Kannauj of Magadh (India), at the request of his brother-in-law, King Songtsen Gampo. With the support of the Paharis and others, he returned to Nepal and regained his father’s throne in 642 AD, and relocate capital to Bhaktapur from Kathmandu. However, his parents, Udaya Deva and Bhadrawati Devi, did not return to Nepal.

Queen Bhrikuti returned to her motherland, Nepal, around 645 AD to meet her brother, King Narendra Deva, travelling through the Kodari Pass. During her visit, she advised her brother to build a palace named “Bhadradhiwas” in honour of their mother, Queen Bhadrawati Devi. The palace is believed to have been built in Bhaktapur, although its historical identification and location require further study and investigation.

In 650 AD, King Songtsen Gampo announced the date and time of his death. According to tradition, Queen Bhrikuti chose voluntary death (स्वेच्छिक मृत्यु) at the age of 25, dying in the king’s lap at the time of his death. It is also believed that Bhrikuti’s body was buried alongside King Songtsen Gampo in the royal burial ground in the Chongye Valley of Lhasa, which is now an important tourist destination.

Exiled Princess Bhrikuti, who carried the Buddhist culture and teachings of the Buddha from her motherland as a spiritual dowry, shared them with her husband, King Songtsen Gampo. Through her influence, these teachings reached the royal palace and capital of Lhasa, spread throughout Tibet, and eventually extended into mainland China and Southeast Asia. Although she lived only a short life, her remarkable contribution and spiritual influence earned her lasting reverence. She came to be venerated as Green Tara, a tradition that was widespread across Tibet and Southeast Asia.

The history of Bhrikuti is not merely a story of the past; it is a history of cultural exchange, resilience, and peace. From the 8th century, Buddhism experienced periods of decline and suppression in Nepal and India, while continuing to flourish in China and other parts of Asia. In Nepal, the revival of Buddhism gained new momentum following the political changes of 1950s in Nepal, strengthened by renewed cultural and intellectual connections with Buddhist communities beyond the Himalayas, especially from mainland China. Bhrikuti’s legacy reminds us that ideas, cultures, and spiritual teachings can cross borders and endure even through the most difficult periods. As a princess who carried the teachings of the Buddha from Nepal to Tibet and beyond, she represents a historic bridge connecting Nepal, Tibet, China, and the wider Buddhist world. Honouring Bhrikuti today would therefore be more than commemorating a historical figure; it would be a celebration of Nepal’s enduring contribution to peace, compassion, cultural dialogue, and friendship in the globe.

—

title: Mountain collapses into river in Nepal landslide - The Telegraph
description: Mountain collapses into river in Nepal landslide  The Telegraph
publisher.title: The Telegraph
full_article:
A mountain has collapsed into a river in Nepal during a wave of landslides and avalanches across the country.

Video footage shows trees and buildings sinking into Kali Gandaki River in Lete village, in the northern Mustang district, on Sunday.

The latest landslide happened as Nepal continues to rebuild a month after a glacial flood killed more than 1,450 people and left more than 6,000 missing. Efforts to recover bodies along the border with Tibet are ongoing.

Since Thursday, heavy rain across the mountain districts has triggered floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to Nepal’s national disaster agency.

At least 56 people were killed because of heavy rainfall that triggered similar natural disasters in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, which shares a border with Nepal.

In a separate incident, 16 climbers are believed to have died after an avalanche hit a camp in the Himalayas.

title: One Month Since the Nepal Floods: We're still delivering critical aid & helping reopen schools - All Hands & Hearts
description: One Month Since the Nepal Floods: We're still delivering critical aid & helping reopen schools  All Hands & Hearts
publisher.title: All Hands & Hearts
full_article:
Our teams in Nepal are out every day, helping displaced families with essential food, safe drinking water, cooking supplies, hygiene and cleaning products, medical and sanitation supplies, and power equipment. We have also begun longer-term support, installing water systems and constructing temporary classrooms as we prepare to help these communities rebuild.

The Response, By the Numbers

 300 educational kits distributed to children in Nuwakot, including school bags, notebooks, pens and pencils, geometry sets, coloring materials, drawing books, pencil cases, and water bottles.

⛺ 1,000 temporary shelters provided to families who lost their homes.

 6,300 people received hygiene kits, including everyday necessities such as soap, toothpaste, toothbrushes, wipes, and toilet paper.

What We Are Doing Now

To address critical water shortages, we have moved from emergency water jugs to establishing drinking-water stations, utility water systems, storage tanks, and filtration systems, while also constructing shower facilities to improve longer-term hygiene and sanitation. Continued deliveries across displacement centers are helping create safer, more dignified living conditions while supporting families through both immediate needs and the longer-term recovery process.

Rebuilding Schools is Critical

Schools are at the heart of strong communities. Right now, more than 300 classrooms have been destroyed or damaged, and the schools that were not damaged have been converted to shelters for displaced families. Getting children back to school is not the final step of recovery. It is one of the things that makes recovery possible.

So far, we’ve provided students with learning kits, early childhood development toys, educational games, and slippers to help them get back to some version of normal. At eight schools, our team disinfected 70 classrooms, preparing spaces for more than 1,000 students and 200 staff members to return. Along the riverbank in Nuwakot, we’re building a secure fence around Chandeswory School to keep children away from unstable ground near the water, a small change that removes one more worry for kids who are already carrying so much.

After recent floodwaters sadly swept away Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, we allocated temporary space to keep learning alive. Our staff, dedicated masons, and volunteers are working side by side to construct three temporary classrooms using two robust truss structures. In addition to the classrooms, we are installing complete plumbing and electrical systems and building dedicated toilet facilities for the students.

This last month, we launched the Back to School Commitment: over the next two years, we aim to raise $5 million to rebuild 20 schools in Nepal communities that need them most. We are grateful to everyone for already helping us raise $1 million toward that goal—but there’s still a long way to go before every one of those schools reopens! Join us in getting kids back into safe, stable classrooms.

title: WFP continues to provide lifeline for thousands one month since the deadly Nepal floods - World Food Program USA
description: WFP continues to provide lifeline for thousands one month since the deadly Nepal floods  World Food Program USA
publisher.title: World Food Program USA
full_article:
KATHMANDU – A month after devastating floods swept through valleys in northern Nepal, World Food Programme (WFP) assistance continues to provide a vital lifeline to affected communities that remain highly vulnerable. Widespread displacement, lost livelihoods, damaged farmland, and disrupted market access are affecting families’ ability to feed themselves properly, without assistance.

In the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, heavily impacted by the mudslide, WFP has been using trucks where roads are accessible and helicopters to reach communities completely cut off due to washed-away roads and bridges.

And for the first time ever in a rapid-onset emergency response, WFP has deployed humanitarian cargo drones to airlift food and relief items to communities where even helicopters cannot land. This has reduced delivery time from days to mere minutes by air.

As part of these response efforts led by the Government of Nepal, WFP has now completed a first round of food assistance, providing more than 15,500 flood-affected people with 127MT of food.

Disasters such as this can further worsen nutrition by disrupting markets, destroying livelihoods, and reducing access to diverse and nutritious foods.

WFP has been carrying out assessments of food security in the affected areas.

The latest monitoring shows that 92 percent of households surveyed reported acceptable food consumption, but nearly all of them are relying on humanitarian assistance for their staple foods.

“While emergency food assistance has protected families from immediate hunger, many households remain highly vulnerable,” said WFP Nepal Representative and Country Director Riaz Lodhi. “WFP is committed to support communities as they transition from relief to recovery, restoring livelihoods and rebuilding communities.”

Besides delivering food assistance to the hardest-to-reach communities, WFP has also offered critical logistics support to the entire humanitarian community.

The WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster in Nepal has served as the backbone of the wider response, offering coordination, handing and delivery for 70 partner organizations.

So far, WFP has moved more than 160 MT of relief items by road and air. These items include medical supplies, tents, solar lamps, blankets, woodstoves, and personal hygiene products.

Also, WFP continues to operate the Kathmandu Humanitarian Staging Area which receives, stores and dispatches all types of humanitarian assistance. It has also established a common humanitarian office and logistics hub in Bidur, Nuwakot. This has brought humanitarian actors closer to affected communities and facilitated the onward delivery of assistance for both immediate relief efforts and longer-term recovery and reconstruction.

The next round of WFP’s assistance in Nepal is being delivered in the form of cash, reaching approximately 38,000 people located in areas where markets are accessible.

For communities which remain completely cut off from access, WFP will continue to provide food assistance for as long as necessary and until market access is re-established.

The international community – from donor countries to individual givers – has responded in a timely and generous manner, allowing WFP to reach people in need quickly and efficiently.

“The response thus far demonstrates what is possible when governments, humanitarian organizations and other donors act together to assist those most in need,” added Lodhi.

WFP may need additional funds for the recovery phase, pending results of current assessments.

The United Nations World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of weather extremes.

New visuals of the aftermath of the avalanche at the Himlung Himal peak in Nepal have emerged, showing the sheer extent of the disaster. The death count from the avalanche has risen to four after two more bodies were recovered on Monday, while eight people remain missing, according to Nepalese officials.

Fresh visuals shot from a hovering helicopter show rescuers standing on a snow-covered slope with their climbing gear and equipment. As the helicopter flies low over the snow, yellow mountain tents buried deep under fresh snow become visible, showing the extent to which the campsite was covered.
